notes.meaning: Solomon wrote this song as the greatest and most excellent of all his compositions. In the traditional Christian understanding, it is the best song because it describes the deep love between Christ and His redeemed people. It gives believers on earth a joyful foretaste of heaven.

differ.view: Some evangelicals hold that the book was written primarily as a literal love poem celebrating human romance and marriage, rather than as an allegory of Christ and the church.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Modern scholars generally reject an allegorical meaning and view the book as ancient Hebrew poetry celebrating human love, or as a drama about a rustic maiden resisting royal seduction.

notes.meaning: The speaker begins with an eager desire for the Bridegroom's presence and affection. His kisses represent the comforting words and promises of pardon that Christ speaks to the soul. Believers find that His love brings far deeper and more lasting joy than any worldly pleasure.

The Bridegroom is praised for his sweet perfumes, which point to the graces of the Holy Spirit poured out on Jesus. His very name, the Messiah or Anointed One, spreads goodness and life everywhere like opened ointment. Pure and devoted believers love Him dearly because of who He is.

The bride asks to be drawn, confessing that a person cannot come to Christ without the help of His Spirit. When He welcomes the believer into close communion with Himself, grief fades away into real rejoicing. God's people eagerly follow Him and value His love above the finest wine.

The speaker addresses the city women, acknowledging her weathered appearance while insisting that she is still lovely. Traditionally, this shows that believers feel dark and stained by their own sins, yet they are made beautiful and accepted through Christ's righteousness. Outwardly they may seem rough like dark goat-hair tents, but inwardly they are like royal curtains.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Commentators read this simply as a sunburnt country girl speaking to the pale court women of Jerusalem about her tanned skin.

notes.meaning: The bride explains that her brothers were harsh with her and forced her to labor outdoors under the hot sun. In a spiritual sense, this pictures how trials and persecution from false brethren bring suffering and may lead believers to neglect their own souls. God's people patiently acknowledge their own faults in times of trouble, trusting in God's mercy.

The bride calls out to her beloved as a shepherd, asking where he pastures his flock and gives them rest during the heat of noon. This pictures a believer seeking Christ as the Good Shepherd for rest and protection during seasons of outward affliction. Faithful souls dread wandering away to follow other teachers or rivals of Christ.

The Shepherd gently tells her to follow the footprints of the sheep and graze her young goats near the shepherds' tents. To find close fellowship with Christ, believers are directed to walk in the well-worn paths of godly Christians before them. They are to attend the regular worship of God and listen to faithful ministers of the Gospel.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars see these lines as an ironic remark from the city chorus, telling the maiden to go back to her country goats if she cannot fit into court life.

notes.meaning: The King compares his love to a noble mare among Pharaoh's royal chariots, highlighting her beauty, speed, and strength. In traditional Christian interpretation, Christ sees His church as spiritually strong and courageous against all enemies. Believers receive boldness from Him to stand firm in times of spiritual conflict.

The King praises the lovely ornaments framing her face and neck, and promises to provide even richer jewelry of gold and silver. Traditionally, these ornaments picture the gifts, virtues, and spiritual graces that Christ bestows on His people. The Lord who begins this good work will continue to add more grace until it is finished.

The bride delights that her fragrant spikenard perfume sends out its scent while the King sits at his table. This represents believers worshiping Christ and enjoying fellowship with Him in sacred ordinances, such as the Lord's Supper. When Christ draws near, the faith and love He has planted in human hearts rise up to honor Him.

The bride compares her beloved to a sachet of fragrant myrrh held close to her heart and a cluster of sweet henna blossoms from En-gedi. For Christians, this pictures Christ as the believer's most treasured possession, held dear through all the dark nights of life's troubles. He brings spiritual comfort and atonement, meaning the way He makes peace between God and sinners.

The Bridegroom praises her beauty again and notes that she has dove-like eyes. Doves' eyes represent a humble, pure, and faithful outlook guided by the Holy Spirit. Christ takes delight in the holy character He creates in the hearts of His people.

The bride returns the praise, confessing that Christ is the truly fair and pleasant one, and that all her beauty comes from Him. She describes their resting place on fresh green grass under rafters of cedar and fir. Spiritually, this points to the peaceful, lasting home believers have in fellowship with Christ under His secure covenant.
